To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hrpX--hrcU operon from E. caratovora subsp carotovora is composed of 15 genes, and that a mutant with a hrpX:: entrancedposon insertion exhibits high basal-level expression from the hrp cluster and reduced virulence.

the hrpX gene of E. carotivora subsp. atroseptica is required for normal virulence in the plant host Arabidopsis thaliana, and that the hrp genes are expressed at high basal level in an hrpX mutant, resulting in reduced virulence.
the hrpX--hrcU genes form an operon, that the hrpXY locus regulates the hrp genes, and that overexpression of the hrp genes reduces virulence in Arabidopsis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the hrp cluster from a soft-rotting pathogen, and with the elucidation of the role of hrp -dependent virulence in this organism.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the type III secretion pathway and the effect of these on the virulence of E. carotova sp. carotova in Arabidopsis plants.

the identification of genes involved in virulence in E. carotivora subsp. atroseptica and E. carototora subsp. betavasculorum, which are closely related to the E. carotovera subsp. carovotora strains studied in the present work.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hrp -dependent pathogenicity of E. carotova subsp. carovovora requires both basal-level and inducible expression of hrp-regulated virulence genes.
hrp genes are necessary for virulence in soft-rot bacteria but not sufficient.
hrp gene expression is necessary but not sufficient for virulence of E. carotivora subsp.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a high level of hrp expression is not necessarily beneficial for the bacterium.
the hrp cluster of E. carotova subsp. carovova contains a large number of genes, which may be involved in the regulation of the type III secretion machinery.
the hrp cluster of E. carot ovora sp. carovora is a complex genetic system, and the expression of its genes must be tightly controlled to ensure optimal virulence.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a better understanding of hrp -mediated virulence mechanisms in E. carotova sp. carotova is needed before we can fully exploit the potential for using hrp genes as virulence determinants in the development of new biocontrol agents.
the expression levels of hrp genes need to be tightly regulated for optimal virulence of E. carotivora sp. carovotova.
the hrp cluster of E. carot ovora subsp. atroseptica is very similar to the hrp cluster in the non-macerating Erwinia sp., and that the hrpX gene is essential for the hrp cluster function.
